summary: Lee Robinson outlines how Cursor trains models through a recursive improvement loop: deploy a model, collect user feedback, improve data and evals, scale compute, and repeat. This is decomposed into an outer loop (feedback, AB tests, online metrics feeding into better evals) and an inner loop (rapidly climbing high-quality evals with difficult RL tasks). The outer loop relies on external user feedback and internal dogfooding, with most revenue coming from agent usage. The inner loop requires high-quality evals modeling real software engineering tasks. Cursor addresses reward hacking (models searching Git history or finding public eval forks) via Git deletion and network allowlists, maintaining Cursor Bench as a private eval set. Ambitious training problems are generated by building complex applications, deleting features so tests fail, and asking models to re-implement them. Textual feedback is a new learning method where a teacher model provides targeted hints at specific points in long RL rollouts, then adjusts token probabilities to shape behavior. Scaling compute is enabled by SpaceX partnership: Colossus supercomputer (100,000 GPUs in 122 days, another 100,000 in 92 days) and Terafab custom chips. Compute is allocated across serving, training (pre-training through RL), data and reward generation, continuous evals, and research experimentation. The goal is multiple simultaneous large training runs with researchers unblocked. Agent-based automation lets researchers run experiments from Slack, with agents creating problems, generating evals, and paging humans when infrastructure fails. The recursive future: each new top-level model enables smarter derivative models for judging, rewards, and data generation, raising the intelligence floor across all loops. Cursor anticipates releasing a new model soon that is a notable improvement over Composer 2.5.

sections.title: Introduction and recursive model improvement overview
sections.summary: Lee Robinson introduces the recursive model improvement loop at Cursor: deploy model, collect feedback, improve data, scale compute, repeat. He notes this serial process is slow and introduces a two-loop framework (outer and inner) to go deeper.

sections.title: Progress and success of Composer 2.5
sections.summary: Composer 2.5, released in May, is now Cursor's most popular model. It is fast, smart, and cost-effective. Cursor's ML team has been building large-scale training for about a year, transitioning from specialized models to state-of-the-art ambitions. Goals for next version include bigger model, full pre-train from scratch, infusing general data, and pushing RL further.

sections.title: Improving the outer loop with user feedback
sections.summary: Most Cursor revenue now comes from agent usage, providing rich training data. External feedback includes thumbs up/down. Internal dogfooding provides manual and automated reports. Combining these over time improves models.

sections.title: Climbing the inner loop with high-quality evals
sections.summary: The inner loop requires high-quality evals that model real software engineering tasks: understanding intent across many files, deciding when to push back vs trust users, and investigating incidents across Datadog, Slack, and Notion. Evals shape desired behaviors.

sections.title: Solving reward hacking in public benchmarks
sections.summary: Models hack public evals by searching Git history or finding forks online. Cursor mitigates this by deleting Git history during evals and applying network allowlists. Cursor Bench is a private eval set based on real engineering tasks held out from training.

sections.title: Scaling training with ambitious problems
sections.summary: As models score 90%+ on evals, those evals must be retired. Creating difficult problems requires research taste and compute. Method: generate complex application, delete a feature so tests fail, ask model to re-implement with verifiable reward.

sections.title: New learning methods: Teacher-student textual feedback
sections.summary: Textual feedback addresses credit assignment in long RL rollouts. A teacher model provides targeted hints at specific points (e.g., reminding about available tools), then token probabilities are upweighted or downweighted to shape behavior. Applicable to tool adherence, style, and any desired behavior.

sections.title: Scaling compute infrastructure with SpaceX and Colossus
sections.summary: Cursor partners with SpaceX for compute access, enabling training of large models from scratch. Colossus supercomputer was built in 122 days for 100,000 GPUs, with another 100,000 added in 92 days. Terafab builds custom chips. This full-stack control from product to chips enables advantageous model training.

sections.title: Understanding compute allocation in model training
sections.summary: Compute is allocated across: serving models to end users and internal checkpoints, AB tests and variations, the training process (pre-training, mid-training, RL), derivative models for inner loop work, data and reward generation, continuous evals on new checkpoints, and research experimentation including side runs. The goal is multiple simultaneous large training runs with researchers unblocked.

sections.title: Agent-based automation and research efficiency
sections.summary: Models with tools and context (Mario analogy: tools make Super Mario, context makes Fire Mario) can use computers, follow Slack threads, and store files. Researchers run experiments directly from Slack via a fleet of agents that create problems, generate evals, and page humans when infrastructure fails. An entire team automates non-ambitious ML research work.

sections.title: The recursive future: Models training models
sections.summary: Each new top-level model enables smarter derivative models for judging, rewards, and data generation, raising the intelligence floor across all loops. The smartest model is the bottleneck; improving it improves every loop. This achieves recursive self-improvement where models improve continuously on your behalf. Robinson concludes by thanking the Cursor team and hinting at a new model release soon.

limitations: The recursive improvement loop is inherently slow and serial, allowing only one big run at a time
Public evals don't reflect true model usage since real users have internet and Git access
Many models today are not very good at complex software engineering tasks like investigating incidents across multiple tools
As models get smarter, eval half-life decreases and evals must be continuously retired and replaced
Bottleneck shifts from compute to human researchers babysitting runs, motivating agent automation
The smartest model in the system is a bottleneck: derivative models for evals, rewards, and data generation are only as good as the top-level model
